title: When to write a script, and in what
summary: A script repeats the same steps every time, without forgetting one. When it's worth writing, and when bash or Python fits the job better.

scheme: a script      write it once, try it on 3,
text: You must rename 300 photos with their date. By hand, it takes an afternoon, and somewhere you will make a typo.
A script is a file of commands that the computer runs for you, in order, the same way every time.
- A good rule: if you did it twice by hand and you'll do it again, write a script.
- A one-time job of three commands doesn't need one.
What you get: the steps live in a file instead of in your memory.
- Nobody skips step 7 on a tired Friday.
- A teammate can read it, review it in git, and run it too.
- A timer can run it at 3 a.m. while you sleep.
What it costs: time to write and test it, and to fix it when the world around it changes.

scheme: real error handling, long code   Python
text: Which language? Pick the one that fits the job.
- Bash is made to run other programs: copy, archive, call tar or rsync, chain commands.
- Python is made to work on data: read JSON, compute, handle each error properly.

- Google's shell style guide says it plainly: past about 100 lines, or once the logic stops being simple, rewrite the script in a more structured language, early, because scripts grow. Python is the usual pick.

scheme: a script repeats mistakes as fast as
1. try it on a copy, or on 3 files
2. make it print what it would do
3. make it stop at the first error
text: One warning before you write your first one: a script does exactly what it says, very fast. A mistake in it hits all 300 files, not one.
- Try it on a copy, or on a few files, first.
- Make it show what it would do before it does it.
- Make it stop at the first error instead of going on.
